title: A hymn in Malar
hookLine: a plea to the clouds not to wait, and Ravidas naming his family's work out loud

cards: Rain, dear cloud. Don't wait even a moment. That's a line from a hymn of Guru Arjan in Malar, in plain English, spoken the way a farmer might speak to a sky that has been holding back.

Rain, beloved, and hold up my mind. A few pages on, in the same raga, a very different voice speaks to the people of his town about his own family and the work they do. Two songs, and what the rain has to do with both.

teach.b: First, the rain. In Guru Arjan's hymn, in paraphrase: rain, dear cloud, don't delay. Rain, beloved, hold up my mind, and let joy and longing fill it.
The cloud stands for God's grace, and the dry field is the mind waiting for it. And the rain doesn't choose which field to fall on.
Now the second voice, one you met on day 774: Ravidas, whose hymns stand near the end of Malar. He speaks to the townspeople and names his caste out loud: a leather worker, known to everyone.
In my heart, he says, I hold the praises of the Lord. In another hymn he goes further. In paraphrase: my family still goes around Benares carrying away dead cattle.
And yet now the learned Brahmins of the city bow before their son, Ravidas, the servant of servants, because he has taken refuge in your Name. In Kedara, at dusk, Ravidas let the labels fade.
Here he says his out loud, in public, and doesn't apologize.
He states the work plainly, work others looked down on, then says what changed: not his birth, not his family's trade, but the Name.

teach.h: NOW THE LEARNED BOW TO HIM.
teach.b: The Gurus placed his words in the Granth, to be sung and bowed to beside their own.
The rain falls on every field alike. The Name, in Ravidas's hymn, falls on a leather worker's son exactly as on anyone.
So a rain song isn't only about weather. It's about grace that doesn't check your family name first. Your line: the rain song.

how: Hymns from the Malar section, the Gurus' and the Bhagats', Ravidas's among them, are sung in kirtan in Raga Malar, and tradition sings them in the rainy season.

games.q: what does “a hymn in malar” mean?
o: a farmer's prayer asking the Lord to end a long drought
Guru Arjan's plea to the rain cloud, and Ravidas's song of grace
Ravidas's apology for the low work his family did

games.q: what's inside the hymns — tap the pairs.

s: Ravidas hides his family's work in his hymns
he names it out loud to the townspeople and says the Name honored him.
the Gurus placed Ravidas's hymns in the Granth beside their own
they're sung and bowed to with the rest of the Granth.
Guru Arjan's rain hymn is only about weather
the cloud stands for grace, and the dry field for the waiting mind.

games.q: you're Ravidas, speaking to the people of your town, who all know your family's work. what do you say?
o: say nothing about where you come from.
name your caste plainly, and the Lord you hold in your heart.
claim you were born into a different family.
games.why: Ravidas names it out loud, and says that through the Name even the learned bow before him.

practice: If you can, play a shabad sung in Malar, or sit in the quiet, and bring to mind someone whose work is easy to overlook: the person who collects your trash, cleans the building, cares for the sick through the night.

Picture rain falling on their roof exactly as it falls on yours, and hold them there with respect for a few slow breaths. If you pray, remember the Name Ravidas took refuge in; if you don't, simply hold the person kindly in mind.

wordCard.voice: A hymn in Malar. Guru Arjan's plea to the cloud not to delay, and Ravidas naming his family's work out loud and saying the Name, not birth, is what honored him. Today's word.

orig.note: megh: cloud; Guru Arjan's Malar hymn calls on the cloud to rain without delay.

carryVoice: Your line: the rain song. Ravidas named his family's work out loud, and didn't apologize. More tomorrow.
